title: Introduction & Chapter 23 (Chemotherapy) Audit Overview
text: Hi, I am Kehinde Abidogun, and this video is about my fact-checking work on chapter 23 of the Med Harvey Cancer textbook, which covers chemotherapy. Chapter 23 was about auditing a textbook. It turned out to be about auditing myself. Chapter 23 is the densest chapter I have worked on so far. It spans seven sections covering the introduction to chemotherapy, principles of treatment, classes of chemotherapeutic agents, pharmacology, drug resistance, side effects, and a summary. The chapter covers 474 sentences, and 136 of them were flagged for verification. Almost every paragraph contains a drug name, a trial result, a dosing formula, or a regulatory fact. I reviewed 86 rows in total. All 21 false verdicts, all 10 flagged verdicts, eight true rows marked for expert review, 15

title: Critical Safety Warning: Venetoclax & Multiple Myeloma Errors
text: Spot-check true rows, all 10 editorial findings, and 22 spot-check DAI only sentences. Of those 86 rows, 52 need revision, and 34 are approved as written. I then audited my own work three separate times, catching errors in my own review before finalizing. The most critical finding involves patient safety. The textbook presents venetoclax for multiple myeloma as established practice, but this use is not FDA approved. The FDA label actually carries a mortality warning against that exact combination. The Canova phase Roman III trial, published in January 2026, missed its primary endpoint and showed more treatment-emergent deaths in the venetoclax arm. This is the kind of error that could directly affect patient care. I also found errors reaching back into the history of chemotherapy. The textbook dates arsenicals to the 1900s,

title: Historical Misconceptions & Methotrexate Dosing Inaccuracies
text: But Heinrich Lissauer treated leukemia with arsenic in 1865, 35 years earlier. It attributes nitrogen mustard research to World War I when it came from World War II. And the methotrexate half-life is stated backwards relative to the FDA label, which matters because rescue timing depends on it. What made this chapter different is the quality control. I ran three full audits. The science, then every source refetched and confirmed on the page, then my deliverables against the instructions. They caught five errors in my own work, including two quotations attributed to the wrong papers and one verdict I reversed myself on dexrazoxane after reading the 2025 evidence. Chapter 23 taught me something important. Auditing AI-generated text is not enough. You also have to audit yourself. text: Happen to the reviewer. That is why I built in multiple passes. One practical flag, files two through five create character encoding defect that corrupts Greek letters. And it is to be fixed before any text edits or find and replace will silently fail. Your turn, take something you have already checked and audit your own audit. Open the source and confirm the exact sentence you quoted is really on the page. Check the checking, that is where my five errors were hiding. I am Kehind Abeitol auditing the Med Harvey Cancer Textbook for Humanitarian's AI.
